lessons.title: Twelve rhythms in words, part one: narrow, irregular, and junctional
lessons.body:
## A second pass, with an action attached

You already know the four questions: rate, regularity, P waves, QRS width. This pass adds the rhythms that live between the famous ones, described in words, each with the **first thing you do**.

### 1. Sinus arrhythmia

Normal-looking beats, upright P before each QRS, narrow, but the R-to-R spacing stretches and shortens in a cycle that matches breathing: faster on inspiration, slower on expiration.

**First action: nothing.** This is a normal variant, common in children and young healthy adults, and it is the single most over-reported strip in a department. Know it so you do not escalate it.

### 2. Premature atrial contraction (PAC)

A beat arrives early. Its P wave looks different from the others, sometimes buried in the previous T wave, and the QRS after it is narrow and normal. The pause afterward is usually **incomplete**, meaning the underlying rhythm resets.

**First action: count them and chart them.** Occasional PACs are common and benign. Frequent PACs are a known warning shot for atrial fibrillation, so the frequency is the useful information at handoff.

### 3. Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

Irregularly irregular, no identifiable P waves, a wavy or flat baseline, ventricular rate over `100` and often `130` to `170`.

**First action: feel a pulse while you look at the screen, and compare the two rates.** In fast atrial fibrillation some beats are too weak to open the aortic valve, so the palpated rate can be much lower than the monitor rate. That gap is the **pulse deficit**, and it tells you the patient is not perfusing every beat. Report both numbers, get a blood pressure, and get a 12-lead.

### 4. Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction

Stubbornly regular, narrow, and almost exactly `150`. That specific number is the tell: the atria are firing near `300` and the ventricles answer every other beat.

**First action: look hard for sawtooth waves before calling it sinus tachycardia**, especially in the inferior leads and V1, and get a 12-lead. Sinus tachycardia at exactly `150` and unvarying, in a patient with no reason to be tachycardic, is flutter until proven otherwise.

### 5. Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Irregularly irregular, rate over `100`, and unlike atrial fibrillation there **are** P waves, with **at least three different shapes**, and varying PR intervals. Classic in the patient with severe COPD who arrives short of breath.

**First action: say what you see in words.** Irregular but there are P waves, and they keep changing shape. That sentence stops the room from treating it as atrial fibrillation.

### 6. Junctional rhythm

Regular, narrow QRS, rate `40` to `60`, with **no visible P wave, an inverted P just before the QRS, or a P hiding right after it**. The atrioventricular junction has taken over because the sinus node stopped or the signal was blocked. Accelerated junctional runs `60` to `100`.

**First action: blood pressure and symptoms, then ask about medications.** Digoxin, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are common causes. A junctional escape at `38` in a lightheaded patient is a different problem from an accelerated junctional at `80` in someone comfortable.

> **Key:** For every rhythm in this set, the first action includes touching the patient. The screen ranks the possibilities; the pulse and the blood pressure decide the urgency.
keyPoints: Sinus arrhythmia varies with respiration, is a normal variant, and should not be escalated.
Frequent premature atrial contractions predict atrial fibrillation, so the useful handoff information is how many.
In fast atrial fibrillation, compare the palpated rate to the monitor rate; the gap is the pulse deficit and signals poor perfusion.
A stubbornly regular narrow rhythm at almost exactly 150 is atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction until sawtooth waves are excluded.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but has P waves of at least three shapes; junctional rhythm is regular at 40 to 60 with absent, inverted or hidden P waves.

checks.q: A monitored patient's R-to-R intervals lengthen and shorten in time with his breathing. P waves are upright and normal. What is this?
choices: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response
Sinus arrhythmia, a normal variant requiring no action
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Second-degree heart block
checks.why: Respiratory variation with normal upright P waves defines sinus arrhythmia, which is normal especially in the young. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves, multifocal atrial tachycardia is fast with changing P shapes, and heart block drops QRS complexes.

checks.q: The monitor reads 148 in atrial fibrillation, but you count a radial pulse of 96. What does this mean?
choices: The monitor is picking up artifact and should be ignored
The pulse oximeter is malfunctioning and should be moved
There is a pulse deficit: some beats are too weak to generate a palpable pulse
The patient has converted to sinus rhythm
checks.why: In fast atrial fibrillation, short filling times leave some beats without enough stroke volume to reach the wrist, producing a pulse deficit. Both numbers are real, and the gap itself is the clinically useful finding to report.

checks.q: A narrow regular rhythm sits at exactly 150 and never varies. What should you consider first?
choices: Sinus tachycardia from anxiety
Atrial flutter conducting 2:1 with an atrial rate near 300
Junctional rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm with premature atrial contractions
checks.why: Sinus tachycardia varies beat to beat with activity and emotion, while flutter with fixed 2:1 conduction parks at almost exactly 150. Junctional rhythms are slow, and premature beats make the rhythm irregular.

lessons.title: Twelve rhythms in words, part two: wide, slow, and blocked
lessons.body:
## The six that change what the room does

### 7. Premature ventricular contraction (PVC)

A beat arrives early, **wide** and bizarre, with no P wave before it, and the T wave usually points opposite to the QRS. The pause afterward is usually **complete**.

Patterns worth naming: **bigeminy** is every other beat, **trigeminy** every third, a **couplet** is two in a row, and three or more in a row is a **run of ventricular tachycardia**. **R-on-T** means a PVC lands on the previous T wave, which can trigger a lethal rhythm.

**First action: pulse and blood pressure, then count.** Report the pattern in words: about six a minute, two couplets, and one landed on a T wave. New frequent PVCs in a chest pain patient go straight to the nurse.

### 8. Wide-complex tachycardia

Fast, wide, usually regular. It may be ventricular tachycardia or a supraventricular rhythm conducted abnormally, and telling them apart is a physician's problem with real diagnostic difficulty.

**First action: treat it as ventricular tachycardia.** Feel a pulse, look at the patient, call for the nurse, put the defibrillator pads on, bring the cart. In an adult with a history of heart disease, a wide regular tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia the large majority of the time, and the cost of the opposite assumption is fatal.

### 9. Torsades de pointes

A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that appears to twist around the baseline: complexes grow tall, shrink, and grow again. It arises from a long QT, which drugs and low potassium and low magnesium cause.

**First action: this is a cardiac arrest rhythm if pulseless.** Check a pulse, call the code, start compressions. Magnesium is the specific treatment and the nurse will want it fast. Look back at the prior tracings for a long QT and say so.

### 10. Idioventricular and agonal rhythm

Wide, slow, `20` to `40`, no P waves, often bizarre and drifting. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm runs `40` to `100` and is a common, usually benign finding just after a blocked artery is reopened.

**First action: pulse.** Wide and slow with no pulse is pulseless electrical activity and a cardiac arrest. Wide and slow with a pulse is a patient about to lose one.

### 11. The atrioventricular blocks

- **First degree.** Every P conducts, but the PR interval is longer than `0.20 s`. No dropped beats. **First action: note it and move on.**
- **Second degree type I (Wenckebach).** The PR interval stretches a little more each beat until one P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts. Group beating, often benign. **First action: chart it and tell the nurse.**
- **Second degree type II.** PR intervals are constant, then a QRS suddenly drops with no warning. This one is dangerous and can progress to complete block. **First action: tell the nurse now and keep the patient on the monitor.**

> **Key:** Type I stretches then drops. Type II drops without warning. Type II is the one that gets a pacemaker.

### 12. Third-degree block and pacemaker problems

In **complete heart block**, P waves march at their own rate and QRS complexes march at theirs, with no relationship between them. The ventricular rate is usually `20` to `40` and the patient is often gray and lightheaded.

**First action: pulse, blood pressure, nurse, pads on.** These patients need pacing.

In a paced rhythm, watch for **failure to capture**: a pacer spike with no QRS following it. **Failure to sense** looks like spikes appearing at random, including on top of T waves.

**First action: report the specific failure.** There are spikes with nothing after them is a sentence that moves a room.
keyPoints: PVC patterns: bigeminy every other beat, couplet is two in a row, three or more is a run, and R-on-T can trigger a lethal rhythm.
Treat any wide regular tachycardia as ventricular tachycardia: pulse, patient, nurse, pads, cart.
Torsades de pointes twists around the baseline, comes from a long QT, and is treated with magnesium.
Second-degree type I stretches the PR then drops a beat; type II drops without warning and is the dangerous one.
In complete heart block P waves and QRS complexes march independently; in a paced rhythm, a spike with no QRS after it is failure to capture.

checks.q: A strip shows PR intervals that lengthen progressively over four beats, then a P wave with no QRS, then the cycle restarts. What is this?
choices: Second-degree AV block type II
Second-degree AV block type I, or Wenckebach
Third-degree AV block
First-degree AV block
checks.why: Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat is the definition of Wenckebach. Type II drops beats with a constant PR, third degree shows no relationship at all between P waves and QRS complexes, and first degree drops nothing.

checks.q: A 66-year-old with prior myocardial infarction develops a wide, regular tachycardia at 175 with a weak pulse. What is your action?
choices: Assume supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy and wait for the 12-lead
Ask the patient to bear down while you find the nurse
Treat it as ventricular tachycardia: stay with him, call the nurse, place pads, bring the cart
Recheck the electrodes before doing anything else
checks.why: A wide regular tachycardia in an adult with structural heart disease is ventricular tachycardia most of the time, and the cost of assuming otherwise is fatal. Vagal maneuvers, delays for a 12-lead, and electrode checks all waste time in a patient with a weak pulse.

checks.q: A paced patient's strip shows vertical spikes that are not followed by any QRS complex. How do you report it?
choices: As artifact from a loose lead wire
As normal pacemaker function
As failure to capture: there are spikes with nothing after them
As a run of ventricular tachycardia
checks.why: A spike without a resulting QRS means the pacemaker fired but the myocardium did not respond, which is failure to capture and needs immediate attention. Artifact does not occur at regular pacing intervals, and no ventricular complexes are present at all.

lessons.title: STEMI mimics, and the false alarm that costs you the next one
lessons.body:
## Two ways to be wrong

A department that activates the cath lab for everything burns a team out and stops responding. A department that hesitates loses muscle. The tech does not adjudicate either way, but you sit at the point where most **manufactured** false alarms are created: a misplaced electrode, a wrong filter, a half-height calibration.

> **Key:** Your job is to remove every artificial reason the tracing looks abnormal, then move it to a provider fast, every single time. Recognizing a mimic makes you better at describing what you see; it never makes you the person who decides.

## The common mimics

**Benign early repolarization.** Young, often male, often athletic. Concave, upward-sloping ST elevation of `1` to `3 mm`, most obvious in V2 to V5, with a notched or slurred J point and tall T waves. **No reciprocal depression**, and the pattern is stable across every prior tracing.

**Acute pericarditis.** **Diffuse** concave ST elevation across many lead groups at once, plus **PR segment depression**, and PR elevation in aVR. No reciprocal depression except in aVR and V1. A real STEMI respects one artery's territory; pericarditis does not respect anatomy at all.

**Left ventricular hypertrophy.** Very tall voltages, with ST depression and T inversion in the lateral leads and **discordant** ST elevation in V1 to V3. Common in longstanding hypertension.

**Left bundle branch block and ventricular paced rhythms.** Both produce a wide QRS with ST segments that normally point **opposite** to the main QRS direction, which looks like elevation. A new bundle branch block with symptoms still gets a provider immediately. Clinicians use the Sgarbossa criteria here: ST elevation of `1 mm` or more **in the same direction** as the QRS, ST depression of `1 mm` or more in V1 to V3 in the same direction, or excessively discordant elevation.

**Hyperkalemia.** Tall, narrow, peaked T waves that look like tents, then a flattened or absent P wave, then a widening QRS, then a sine wave. This is a mimic that is its own emergency.

**Brugada pattern, Takotsubo, ventricular aneurysm, and hypothermia** round out the list. A ventricular aneurysm shows persistent elevation with deep Q waves and no change across serial tracings. Hypothermia shows the **Osborn J wave**, a hump at the end of the QRS.

## The ones that are real and look small

Missing these is the more expensive error.

- **Hyperacute T waves.** Broad, tall, symmetric T waves are often the earliest STEMI change, before any elevation appears.
- **Wellens pattern.** Deep symmetric T wave inversion, or biphasic T waves, in V2 and V3, in a patient who is **currently pain free**. It signals a critically narrowed left anterior descending artery. Pain free is not safe here.
- **de Winter pattern.** Upsloping ST depression at the J point in the precordial leads with tall symmetric T waves, equivalent to an anterior STEMI.
- **ST elevation in aVR with widespread depression.** Suggests left main or severe three-vessel disease.
- **Posterior infarct.** ST **depression** in V1 to V3 with tall R waves. Covered in its own lesson.

## What you actually do

Rule out your own contribution first: count the ribs, confirm the calibration pulse is full height, confirm `25 mm/s` and `10 mm/mV`, confirm the diagnostic filter, and confirm limb electrodes are on limbs. Then hand the tracing to a provider and say what you see in plain description, not diagnosis.

> **On shift:** The correct sentence is never I think this is pericarditis. It is this has elevation in a lot of leads and the patient is 26 with chest pain worse lying flat, can you look now.
keyPoints: The tech never adjudicates a mimic; the job is to remove artificial causes of abnormality and move the tracing to a provider fast every time.
Early repolarization is concave with a notched J point and no reciprocal change; pericarditis is diffuse with PR depression and ignores arterial territory.
Left ventricular hypertrophy, left bundle branch block and paced rhythms all create discordant ST elevation, which Sgarbossa criteria address.
Hyperkalemia mimics ischemia with peaked T waves, a vanishing P wave, a widening QRS, then a sine wave, and is itself an emergency.
Hyperacute T waves, the Wellens pattern in a pain-free patient, de Winter upsloping depression, and aVR elevation with diffuse depression are real and easy to miss.

checks.q: A 62-year-old is pain free now after two episodes of chest pain. His ECG shows deep symmetric T wave inversions in V2 and V3. What does this suggest?
choices: Benign early repolarization, since he is currently asymptomatic
A Wellens pattern, indicating critical left anterior descending narrowing despite being pain free
Pericarditis, because the changes are anterior
Artifact from V2 and V3 placed too high
checks.why: Deep symmetric or biphasic T inversions in V2 and V3 during a pain-free interval is the Wellens pattern and predicts a critical proximal lesion. Early repolarization elevates rather than inverts, pericarditis is diffuse with PR depression, and high V1 and V2 placement inverts P waves rather than producing deep symmetric T inversions.

checks.q: A 26-year-old has concave ST elevation in V2 through V5 with a notched J point, tall T waves, and no reciprocal depression. Prior tracings look identical. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Anterior STEMI requiring immediate activation
Benign early repolarization
Hyperkalemia
Left bundle branch block
checks.why: Concave elevation with a notched J point, no reciprocal change, and an identical prior tracing is the early repolarization pattern. A STEMI evolves and usually produces reciprocal depression, hyperkalemia peaks the T waves and flattens P waves, and bundle branch block widens the QRS.

checks.q: Before handing off a tracing with apparent ST elevation, which self-check is most important?
choices: Confirm the interpretive statement printed by the machine
Switch to the 40 Hz filter to clean the baseline
Confirm rib count, full-height calibration pulse, 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV, and limb electrodes on limbs
Compare it with a tracing from a different patient with the same complaint
checks.why: Misplacement, half-height calibration and non-standard speed all manufacture apparent ST changes, so removing your own contribution comes first. The machine statement is not verification, the 40 Hz filter can distort ST segments, and another patient's tracing is irrelevant.

lessons.title: Artifact rounds: six tracings and what went wrong
lessons.body:
## Working the cases

Each case gives what you saw. Decide the cause and the fix before reading on. The pattern to build is: **which electrode, or which piece of the environment, could produce exactly this and nothing else.**

### Case 1

A 12-lead on a diaphoretic chest pain patient. Leads I, II and aVR look fine. Lead III and aVF have a thick fuzzy baseline that drifts with each breath. V leads are clean.

**Cause: the left leg electrode.** III and aVF are the two leads that use LL most heavily, and only those are affected. **Fix:** dry the skin, new electrode from a sealed pack, press the edges, drape the cable so it is not pulling.

### Case 2

The monitor alarms VTACH on bed 9. On the screen the complexes are wide and chaotic at about `180`. You look in: the patient is sitting up brushing his teeth and looks at you.

**Cause: motion artifact from the brushing arm.** **Fix:** none needed clinically. Confirm a pulse, tell him to pause for ten seconds, watch the baseline return. Then reset the alarm and tell the nurse you checked it. A checked alarm that is documented is not a nuisance alarm.

### Case 3

Limb leads look perfect. V1 through V6 are all present but tiny, with almost no R wave growth across the chest.

**Cause: electrodes placed on top of breast tissue, or dry gel.** Tissue between the electrode and the heart attenuates the signal and fakes poor R wave progression. **Fix:** place V3 through V6 under the breast against the chest wall, with fresh electrodes, and repeat.

### Case 4

Lead II is a nearly flat line, but the patient has a strong pulse of `82` and leads I and III look normal.

**Cause: right arm and right leg electrodes reversed.** Lead II is a comparison between RA and LL, and swapping in the ground reference collapses it. **Fix:** check the four limb wires against the colors, correct them, and repeat the tracing. Never chart a flat lead as asystole when other leads are normal.

### Case 5

A clean tracing at 0200. At 0215 a repeat shows a perfectly regular fuzzy thickening across every lead. Between the two, a forced-air warming blanket was started.

**Cause: `60 Hz` alternating-current interference from nearby powered equipment.** **Fix:** move or unplug the non-essential device, separate the ECG cable from power cords, untangle the lead wires, confirm the ground electrode is on, and repeat. Reach for the notch filter only after the physical fixes.

### Case 6

A 74-year-old with Parkinson disease. The machine prints `ATRIAL FIBRILLATION`, but the ventricular complexes are perfectly regular and there is fine rapid fuzz across the baseline that could be mistaken for fibrillatory waves.

**Cause: tremor artifact read as fibrillation by the algorithm.** **Fix:** warm the patient, support the arms on the bed or pillows so they are not held up against gravity, ask him to relax, and if it persists move the limb electrodes proximally to the shoulders and hips and **write torso placement on the tracing**. Regular R-to-R intervals are the giveaway: atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular.

> **Trap:** Every one of these six had a physical cause and a physical fix. Reaching for a filter first hides the evidence and can hide real findings with it.

## The general method

1. Which leads are affected? One electrode, one limb, one region, or everything?
2. Does the artifact have a pulse? Match the screen against the patient.
3. What changed in the room in the last five minutes?
4. Fix the physical cause, repeat the tracing, and label anything non-standard you had to do.
keyPoints: Artifact confined to III and aVF points at the left leg electrode; a flat lead II with normal I and III points at a right arm and right leg reversal.
Chaotic complexes in a patient who is awake and moving is motion artifact; confirm a pulse, pause the movement, and document that you checked.
Small V leads with poor R wave progression usually mean electrodes on top of breast tissue or dried gel.
Regular fuzzy thickening across every lead after new equipment arrives is 60 Hz interference; fix it physically before using a filter.
Tremor artifact can make an algorithm print atrial fibrillation, but regular R-to-R intervals disprove it.

checks.q: Only leads III and aVF show a fuzzy, drifting baseline. Everything else is clean. Which electrode is the problem?
choices: Right arm
Left arm
Left leg
The V1 chest electrode
checks.why: III and aVF are the leads most dependent on the left leg electrode, so isolated artifact in exactly those two localizes to LL. A right or left arm problem would corrupt lead I and aVR or aVL, and a chest electrode affects only its own V lead.

checks.q: Lead II is nearly flat while leads I and III look normal and the patient has a strong pulse. What do you do?
choices: Document asystole in lead II and notify the nurse
Check the limb wires for a right arm and right leg reversal, correct it, and repeat
Increase the gain to 20 mm/mV and reprint
Switch to the 40 Hz filter
checks.why: Lead II compares the right arm to the left leg, so swapping the right arm with the ground reference collapses it while other leads stay normal. Charting asystole on a perfusing patient is dangerous, and changing gain or filters does not correct a wiring error.

checks.q: What is the correct general order when troubleshooting artifact?
choices: Apply a filter first, then investigate if the artifact persists
Identify which leads are affected, confirm against the patient, fix the physical cause, then repeat and label
Reprint three times and choose the cleanest tracing
Move all limb electrodes to the torso as a first step
checks.why: Localizing by affected leads points to the specific electrode or environmental source, and physical fixes preserve real diagnostic detail. Filters can hide genuine ST findings, repeated reprinting without a fix wastes the clock, and torso placement alters a diagnostic tracing.

lessons.title: Pediatric ECGs: placement, normal findings, and the crying problem
lessons.body:
## The same landmarks, smaller

The bones are the same bones. Find the sternal angle, step onto the second rib, count down to the fourth intercostal space. The spacing is just tighter, so use **pediatric electrodes**, which are smaller and less sticky, and trim rather than overlap if two would touch.

One placement difference matters: many pediatric protocols record **V4R in place of V3**, or add V4R to the standard twelve, because the right ventricle is a much larger part of a child's heart. V4R is the mirror of V4: **`5th` intercostal space, right midclavicular line.** Label the tracing so the reader knows which lead is which.

## Normal in a child, alarming in an adult

A child's heart is built differently and the tracing shows it. These are the findings that get wrongly escalated.

- **Right axis deviation in the newborn.** In the womb the right ventricle does most of the work, so a neonate's axis points right. It migrates leftward over the first months.
- **T wave inversion in V1 to V3.** Normal from about the first week of life through adolescence, and it can persist into young adulthood, where it is called the **juvenile T wave pattern**. Inverted T waves in the right precordial leads of a 9-year-old are expected.
- **An upright T wave in V1 in a one-week-old to seven-year-old is the abnormal finding**, not the inverted one. The direction flips shortly after birth.
- **Short intervals.** Infant PR intervals run roughly `0.08` to `0.12 s` and QRS durations under about `0.08 s`. Applying adult cutoffs will make you call normal children abnormal.
- **Prominent sinus arrhythmia.** Marked respiratory variation is normal and common.
- **Higher rates across the board.** A sinus tachycardia in an infant can reach `220`.

## The rate question that matters

Distinguishing sinus tachycardia from supraventricular tachycardia in a child is a real clinical decision, and the rough guides are useful to know.

| Finding | Sinus tachycardia | Supraventricular tachycardia |
|---|---|---|
| Infant rate | usually under `220` | usually over `220` |
| Child rate | usually under `180` | usually over `180` |
| P waves | present, normal shape | absent or abnormal |
| Variability | rate varies with activity, crying, fever | fixed, almost metronomic |
| History | fever, pain, dehydration, blood loss | abrupt onset, often none |

**A rate that does not budge at all is the strongest clue.** Sinus tachycardia wobbles. Supraventricular tachycardia does not.

## Two findings that make a provider move

**Delta wave and short PR** suggests Wolff-Parkinson-White, a bypass tract around the AV node, and it matters in any child with palpitations or a family history.

**A long QT interval** is screened for in any child with exertional syncope, seizures, or a family history of sudden death or drowning. The corrected QT thresholds used in practice sit around `460` to `480 ms`, and the interpretation belongs to the provider.

## Getting a clean tracing on a child

A crying, struggling child produces an unreadable tracing, and holding them down makes it worse and costs their trust for everything afterward.

1. Warm the room and warm your hands. Cold makes children tense.
2. Let a parent hold the child or sit beside the bed. Explain to the parent first; the child watches the parent's face.
3. Show the electrode on your own arm, or on a stuffed animal, before it touches them.
4. Place everything before you press record, then record during a quiet ten seconds. Wait for the quiet rather than fighting for it.
5. Never call it a sticker that will not hurt if it will pull on removal. Use adhesive remover or warm water, and take them off slowly.

> **On shift:** Ten seconds is all you need. Spend two minutes buying those ten seconds and you will not repeat the tracing three times.
keyPoints: Pediatric protocols commonly record V4R in place of or in addition to V3, at the 5th intercostal space right midclavicular line, and the tracing must be labeled.
Right axis deviation in a newborn and T wave inversion in V1 to V3 through adolescence are normal; an upright T in V1 in a young child is the abnormal finding.
Infant PR intervals run about 0.08 to 0.12 s and QRS under about 0.08 s, so adult cutoffs will falsely flag normal children.
Sinus tachycardia varies and stays under about 220 in infants and 180 in children; supraventricular tachycardia is fixed, metronomic and faster.
A short PR with a delta wave suggests Wolff-Parkinson-White, and a long corrected QT is screened for after exertional syncope or a family history of sudden death.

checks.q: A 9-year-old's ECG shows inverted T waves in V1 through V3. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: An acute anterior ischemic pattern requiring immediate activation
The juvenile T wave pattern, a normal finding at this age
Evidence that V1 and V2 were placed too high
A sign of right ventricular hypertrophy in all cases
checks.why: T wave inversion in the right precordial leads is normal from infancy through adolescence and often into young adulthood. High V1 and V2 placement inverts P waves rather than producing the expected juvenile pattern, and this finding alone does not establish hypertrophy.

checks.q: A 6-month-old has a narrow-complex rate of 238 that has not varied at all in ten minutes, with no visible P waves. What does this favor?
choices: Sinus tachycardia from fever
Supraventricular tachycardia
Normal infant heart rate
Artifact from crying
checks.why: A fixed rate over 220 in an infant with absent P waves favors supraventricular tachycardia, because sinus tachycardia varies with state and rarely exceeds 220. Crying artifact distorts the baseline rather than producing regular narrow complexes at a fixed rate.

checks.q: Where does V4R go on a pediatric tracing?
choices: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border
5th intercostal space, right midclavicular line
Midaxillary line on the right, level with V6
Directly over the sternum at the 5th intercostal space
checks.why: V4R mirrors V4 across the chest, so it sits at the 5th intercostal space in the right midclavicular line. The 4th space at the right sternal border is V1, and the right midaxillary position would be V6R.

lessons.title: The extra leads: posterior and right-sided walkthroughs
lessons.body:
## Why twelve views are not enough

The standard twelve leads look at the front, the left side and the bottom of the heart. Two regions are covered poorly: the **back wall** and the **right ventricle**. Both can infarct, and both are missed on a standard tracing unless somebody goes looking.

## Posterior infarction: reading the mirror

Nothing on the standard twelve leads points at the back wall, so a posterior infarct shows up **backwards** in the leads that face it from the front. In V1, V2 and V3 you see:

- ST **depression** instead of elevation
- **Tall R waves** instead of deep S waves
- **Upright, prominent T waves**
- An R wave that is wider than `0.04 s` and taller than the S wave in V2

That combination in a chest pain patient is a posterior STEMI until a posterior tracing says otherwise. It is frequently called ischemia and treated as a non-ST-elevation event, which delays opening an artery that is completely blocked.

### Placing V7 to V9

All three sit at the **same horizontal level as V6**, wrapping around the left side.

| Lead | Position |
|---|---|
| V7 | Posterior axillary line, level with V6 |
| V8 | Tip of the left scapula, level with V6 |
| V9 | Left border of the spine, level with V6 |

Most machines have only six chest cables, so the usual method is to **move V4, V5 and V6 to the V7, V8 and V9 positions** and reprint, then relabel by hand. Write it clearly: `V4 = V7, V5 = V8, V6 = V9`, or the reader will believe those are the standard positions.

**The threshold is lower back there.** Because the signal crosses more tissue, `0.5 mm` of elevation in a single posterior lead is considered diagnostic, compared with `1 mm` in two contiguous standard leads.

Roll the patient toward you with help, place the three electrodes, and either roll them back onto their side or sit them forward for the ten seconds of recording. Keep the monitor on during the roll.

## Right-sided ECG: the preload trap

When the inferior leads II, III and aVF show elevation, the culprit is usually the right coronary artery, and a large minority of those infarcts, commonly quoted around `40 percent`, involve the **right ventricle**.

That changes treatment immediately. A damaged right ventricle cannot generate pressure on its own; it depends on being filled. **Nitroglycerin drops preload and can cause profound hypotension in these patients.** The treatment is fluid, not vasodilation.

### The key lead

**V4R: `5th` intercostal space, right midclavicular line.** Elevation of `0.5 mm` in V4R supports right ventricular involvement, again a lower threshold than the standard leads.

A full right-sided tracing mirrors all six positions across the chest: V1R through V6R, with V1R and V2R simply swapping the V1 and V2 positions.

**Label it clearly as right-sided.** An unlabeled right-sided tracing looks like dextrocardia to the next reader, and comparing it to the previous standard tracing manufactures a dramatic change that is pure geometry.

> **Key:** In many departments, inferior ST elevation triggers a right-sided tracing automatically. Learn whether yours does, and offer it before you are asked.

## Keeping both tracings

The extra tracing supplements the standard twelve, it never replaces it. Both go in the chart, both are timed and initialed, and the standard one is what the next tracing gets compared against.

> **On shift:** The whole procedure is about ninety seconds once you have done it twice. Practice the electrode moves on a colleague so the first real one is not the first one.
keyPoints: A posterior infarct appears as ST depression with tall R waves and upright T waves in V1 to V3, the mirror image of elevation.
V7, V8 and V9 sit at the V6 horizontal level at the posterior axillary line, the scapular tip and beside the spine, usually by moving V4 to V6 and relabeling.
Posterior and right-sided leads use a lower threshold: 0.5 mm of elevation is considered diagnostic.
V4R is the 5th intercostal space at the right midclavicular line; inferior elevation involves the right ventricle roughly 40 percent of the time.
Right ventricular infarction is preload dependent, so nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension and fluids are given instead.

checks.q: A chest pain tracing shows ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. What should you anticipate?
choices: A request for posterior leads V7 to V9, because this is the mirror image of a posterior infarct
A request for a right-sided tracing with V4R
That the anterior leads were placed too high
That no further tracings are needed since there is no elevation
checks.why: Depression with tall R waves in the right precordial leads is the front-facing mirror of posterior elevation, so posterior leads are the confirming study. Right-sided leads follow inferior elevation, and treating the absence of elevation as reassurance is exactly how a posterior occlusion gets delayed.

checks.q: You move V4, V5 and V6 to the posterior positions and reprint. What must you do?
choices: Nothing; the machine records the change automatically
Discard the original standard tracing to avoid confusion
Hand-label the tracing to show that V4, V5 and V6 are now V7, V8 and V9, and keep both tracings
Set the filter to 40 Hz because posterior signals are weaker
checks.why: The machine has no way to know the electrodes moved, so unlabeled posterior leads will be read as standard positions. The original tracing remains the comparison standard, and changing the filter distorts ST segments rather than improving posterior sensitivity.

checks.q: An inferior STEMI is identified and V4R shows 0.5 mm of elevation. Why does this change management?
choices: It confirms the tracing was recorded at the wrong paper speed
It indicates right ventricular involvement, which is preload dependent, so nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension
It means the patient has dextrocardia
It lowers the urgency because the right ventricle recovers well
checks.why: A right ventricle that cannot generate pressure depends on filling, so vasodilation drops cardiac output sharply and fluid is the treatment. Dextrocardia produces a global pattern rather than isolated V4R elevation, and right ventricular involvement raises rather than lowers the stakes.

lessons.title: Machine settings: speed, gain, filters, and the data you type in
lessons.body:
## Three numbers printed on every tracing

Before reading anything, read the footer. Nearly every machine prints the paper speed, the gain, and the filter settings along the bottom, and all three change what the waveform looks like.

**Paper speed.** `25 mm/s` is standard. At `50 mm/s` every complex is twice as wide, which makes a normal rate look bradycardic and a normal QRS look wide. It is occasionally used deliberately to inspect closely spaced P waves. Always note it.

**Gain, also called sensitivity.** `10 mm/mV` is standard: ten small boxes tall equals one millivolt. Two non-standard settings exist for real reasons.

- **Half standard, `5 mm/mV`**, keeps very tall complexes from overlapping each other, common in left ventricular hypertrophy. It also **halves every ST deviation on the page**, so `2 mm` of real elevation prints as `1 mm`.
- **Double standard, `20 mm/mV`**, enlarges very small complexes and doubles apparent ST changes.

The **calibration pulse** at the start of the tracing proves which setting was used. A full-height rectangular pulse ten small boxes tall means standard. Half height means half standard. Check it before comparing two tracings.

> **Trap:** A machine left on half standard by the previous user will make a real STEMI look borderline. The calibration pulse is the only thing that tells you, and it takes one second to look.

## Filters, and what each one removes

Three filters run on most machines, and each cuts a different part of the signal.

| Filter | Typical settings | What it removes | The cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low-pass, the high-frequency cutoff | `150 Hz` diagnostic adult, `250 Hz` for children, `40 Hz` monitor mode | Muscle tremor and fine noise | `40 Hz` shaves real QRS detail and can attenuate or distort ST segments |
| High-pass, the low-frequency cutoff | `0.05 Hz` diagnostic, `0.5 Hz` monitor mode | Baseline wander | `0.5 Hz` distorts the ST segment, producing artificial depression or elevation |
| Notch, the AC filter | `60 Hz` in the United States, `50 Hz` elsewhere | Building power interference | Slight loss of fine detail |

**Diagnostic mode is `0.05` to `150 Hz` for adults**, and children need the higher upper cutoff because their signals contain faster components. Monitor mode exists to keep a telemetry display stable, and a tracing acquired in monitor mode is not a diagnostic tracing.

> **Key:** If you change any filter to make a tracing readable, write it on the paper. An unlabeled `40 Hz` tracing can hide the finding somebody is looking for.

## The data you type in changes the printed interpretation

The interpretive algorithms use **age and sex** in their thresholds. The V2 and V3 ST elevation criteria differ by sex and by age: `2 mm` in men `40` and over, `2.5 mm` in men under `40`, `1.5 mm` in women. Enter a woman as male, or leave the default `50-year-old male`, and the software applies the wrong cutoff and may print a different conclusion.

Type the real age, the real sex, and the patient identifiers. A tracing labeled with default demographics is also a tracing that can be filed on the wrong chart.

## Acquisition, and what the printed layout hides

Modern machines acquire all twelve leads **simultaneously** for about `10 seconds`, then print them in four columns of `2.5 seconds` each with one or more continuous rhythm strips along the bottom.

The consequence catches people out: an ectopic beat that occurred in the first `2.5 seconds` prints only in the first column, so it appears to be in leads I, II and III only. It is not a regional finding. The rhythm strip along the bottom is the continuous record, which is why it is there.

## Machine housekeeping

Check at the start of every shift: plugged in and charged, paper loaded with a spare roll, cables untangled and inspected for cracks, a sealed pack of fresh electrodes, and the date and time set correctly. **A wrong clock corrupts every door-to-ECG measurement and every serial comparison.** Wipe the cables and the machine between patients per your infection control policy.
keyPoints: Read the footer first: paper speed, gain and filter settings all change how the waveform looks.
Standard is 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV; half standard halves every ST deviation and the calibration pulse is the only proof of which was used.
Diagnostic filtering is 0.05 to 150 Hz for adults and up to 250 Hz for children; monitor mode settings distort ST segments and must be labeled if used.
Age and sex entered into the machine change the interpretive thresholds, including the sex- and age-specific V2 and V3 criteria.
All twelve leads are acquired simultaneously but printed in 2.5-second columns, so an ectopic beat appears only in the column where it occurred.

checks.q: The calibration pulse on a tracing is only five small boxes tall. What does this mean?
choices: The paper speed was set to 50 mm/s
The machine was set to half standard gain, so every amplitude including ST deviation prints at half its true size
The high-pass filter was set to 0.5 Hz
The tracing is uninterpretable and must be discarded
checks.why: A half-height calibration pulse indicates 5 mm/mV, which halves every voltage on the page and can make a real STEMI look borderline. Paper speed changes horizontal width, filter settings do not change the calibration pulse height, and the tracing is usable once the setting is known.

checks.q: Why does entering the patient's correct age and sex matter on the ECG machine?
choices: It only affects how the tracing is filed
The interpretive algorithm applies sex- and age-specific thresholds, including the V2 and V3 ST elevation criteria
It changes the paper speed automatically
It determines which filter the machine selects
checks.why: Thresholds differ by sex and age, such as 2 mm in men 40 and over, 2.5 mm in men under 40 and 1.5 mm in women, so wrong demographics can change the printed conclusion. Filing matters too, but speed and filters are set independently.

checks.q: A single premature beat appears only in the first column of leads I, II and III. What does that indicate?
choices: The ectopic beat originated in the inferior wall
The tracing has a lead reversal
The beat occurred during the first 2.5 seconds, which is the only window those leads printed
The gain was set too high in those leads
checks.why: The twelve leads are acquired simultaneously but printed in sequential 2.5-second columns, so a beat shows only in the column covering its moment. The continuous rhythm strip at the bottom exists precisely to capture the whole recording.

lessons.title: Serial tracings and troponin timing: five cases
lessons.body:
## Why one tracing is never the answer

About a third of myocardial infarctions look normal on the first tracing, and a completely blocked artery can produce a clean ECG for a while. What makes the ECG powerful is **change over time** paired with a blood test that rises over time.

Repeat the tracing every `15` to `30 minutes` while chest pain continues, and **immediately** whenever the pain changes, the vital signs change, the rhythm changes, or the patient says something is different. Write the **pain score on each tracing** so the clinician can pair the picture with the symptom.

## The troponin clock

Troponin is a protein released by dying heart muscle. High-sensitivity assays detect it within an hour or two of injury, which is why timing and **the change between values** matter more than a single number.

- **High-sensitivity troponin** is commonly drawn at `0` and `1 hour`, or `0` and `2` or `3 hours`, depending on the assay and the protocol your lab runs.
- **Conventional troponin** is typically drawn at `0`, `3` and `6 hours`.
- The **delta**, the rise or fall between draws, is what separates an acute injury from a chronically elevated baseline seen in kidney disease and heart failure.

Your part is exact: draw on time, label the **exact collection time**, and hand-walk or fast-track it. A second troponin drawn `40 minutes` late is not a one-hour value and the algorithm cannot use it.

## The cases

### Case 1

58-year-old man, `45 minutes` of pressure, first ECG completely normal, pain `8/10`. You repeat at `20 minutes` because the pain is unchanged: `2 mm` of elevation in II, III and aVF with depression in I and aVL.

**Lesson: the repeat is the test.** Without it he waits for a troponin that may be an hour from rising.

### Case 2

63-year-old woman whose pain resolved after nitroglycerin. Her tracing shows deep symmetric T inversions in V2 and V3. Everyone relaxes because she feels better.

**Lesson: pain free is not safe.** This is the Wellens pattern, which signals a critically narrowed left anterior descending artery and typically shows up during the pain-free window. Hand the tracing over with the words she is pain free now and this is new.

### Case 3

45-year-old, symptom onset `6 hours` ago, ECG normal, initial high-sensitivity troponin below the limit of detection.

**Lesson: even a very low initial value follows a protocol.** Some pathways allow a single-sample rule-out only when onset was well over `3 hours` ago and the value is below a specified threshold. Most still require the second draw. You do not decide which; you draw the second one on time unless the order is cancelled.

### Case 4

72-year-old, ECG unchanged across three tracings, troponin `55` at time zero and `240` at one hour.

**Lesson: the ECG is not the only clock.** A rising delta with a normal ECG is a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He is admitted and heading to the catheterization laboratory, just not in the next ten minutes.

### Case 5

68-year-old with a ventricular paced rhythm and ongoing chest pain. The tracing is hard to read because pacing distorts the ST segments.

**Lesson: when the ECG is unreliable, the serial troponin carries more of the weight.** Draw on time, keep repeating tracings anyway so any new change is captured, and say out loud that the patient is paced so the provider reads it correctly.

> **Key:** Serial means on a clock, not eventually. A tracing at `15` minutes and a troponin at exactly `60` minutes are two of the most concrete things a tech contributes to a chest pain evaluation.
keyPoints: About a third of infarcts have a normal first tracing, so repeat every 15 to 30 minutes during ongoing pain and immediately on any change.
Write the pain score on every tracing so the picture can be paired with the symptom.
High-sensitivity troponin is commonly drawn at 0 and 1 hour, conventional at 0, 3 and 6 hours, and the delta matters more than a single value.
A late second troponin is not a one-hour value and the rule-out algorithm cannot use it.
A pain-free patient with deep symmetric T inversions in V2 and V3 is high risk, and a paced or bundle-blocked tracing shifts weight onto the serial troponin.

checks.q: A chest pain patient's first ECG is normal and his pain is unchanged at 8 out of 10 after 20 minutes. What should happen?
choices: Wait for the first troponin result before repeating the tracing
Repeat the 12-lead now, since roughly a third of infarcts are normal on the first tracing
Repeat the tracing only if the pain worsens
Switch to continuous monitoring instead of repeating a 12-lead
checks.why: Serial tracings during ongoing pain are the standard, and a dynamic change may appear long before a troponin rises. Waiting for a laboratory result, requiring worsening pain, or substituting the monitor all delay a finding the repeat would have caught.

checks.q: Why does the exact collection time on a troponin tube matter so much?
choices: It determines which tube color the lab uses
The rule-in and rule-out algorithms depend on a defined interval, so a late draw is not a one-hour value
It affects the hemolysis rate of the specimen
It changes the reference range the laboratory applies
checks.why: Modern pathways compare values across a specified interval, so a sample drawn 40 minutes late cannot be interpreted as a one-hour result. Tube selection, hemolysis and reference ranges are unrelated to the collection timestamp.

checks.q: A patient with a ventricular paced rhythm has ongoing chest pain and a difficult-to-read tracing. What is the correct approach?
choices: Stop repeating tracings since pacing makes them uninterpretable
Keep obtaining serial tracings, draw serial troponins on time, and state clearly that the patient is paced
Turn off the pacemaker to obtain a clean tracing
Use the 40 Hz filter to remove the pacing spikes
checks.why: Pacing distorts ST segments but does not make tracings worthless, and new changes still matter, so serial tracings continue while the troponin carries more weight. Pacemakers are never disabled by a tech, and filtering out spikes hides clinically important information.

lessons.title: Door to cath lab: walking the protocol and owning the handoff
lessons.body:
## The whole timeline on one page

| Clock | Target | Who |
|---|---|---|
| `0 min` | Arrival, quick registration | Triage, registration |
| Under `10 min` | 12-lead acquired **and in a provider's hands** | Tech |
| Within minutes | Provider interprets, calls the activation | Provider |
| `20` to `30 min` | Catheterization team in house | Cardiology |
| `90 min` | **Door to balloon** at a hospital with a catheterization laboratory | Whole system |
| `120 min` | First medical contact to device when transfer is required, with a **door-in-door-out** target of `30 min` | Whole system |
| `30 min` | Thrombolytics from arrival if no catheterization is available in time | Whole system |

When EMS transmits a field 12-lead and activates from the scene, the patient may bypass the ED entirely. That is why the crew's tracing matters and why it goes in the chart.

## Your task list the moment a STEMI is called

1. **Repeat the 12-lead** if the existing one is more than a few minutes old or anything changed.
2. **Defibrillator pads on**, in the position your department uses, and the monitor on.
3. **Full vitals**, and a blood pressure in both arms if a dissection has not been excluded.
4. **Two intravenous lines** with the nurse, ideally `18 G` or larger. Ask which arm the catheterization team wants left free, because radial access on that side needs an unpunctured wrist and forearm.
5. **Labs** including a type and screen, sent fast.
6. **Remove metal and jewelry**, and cut clothing rather than wrestling it off.
7. **Nothing by mouth.**
8. **Prepare the bed and the route**: oxygen cylinder on the bed, monitor transportable, elevator or hallway cleared.
9. **Copies of every tracing go with the patient**, including the EMS strip.
10. Groin and wrist preparation only if your protocol directs it and someone has ordered it.

> **Key:** The measured interval is door to **balloon**, not door to bed. Everything you do is either shortening that line or not.

## Documenting a tracing so it can be trusted

Every tracing carries the patient's full name, a second identifier, the date, the **exact time**, and your initials. Then, anything non-standard, written by hand on the paper:

- **Right-sided** or **posterior**, with the lead relabeling spelled out
- **Limb leads on torso** and why
- **Filter or gain changed from standard** and why
- **Position** if not supine, such as semi-Fowler's for a patient who cannot lie flat
- **Oxygen device and flow rate**, if any
- **The pain score at the moment of acquisition**

An unlabeled variation is worse than no tracing, because it will be compared against a standard one and the difference will be read as a change in the patient.

## The handoff sentence

Hand the paper to a person. Do not leave it on a counter, in a printer tray, in a chart rack, or on a keyboard. Then say four things in one breath:

**Who, what you saw, when, and what you want.**

For example: bed 4, the 58-year-old with chest pressure, this is his tracing from two minutes ago, there is elevation in two, three and aVF, can you look now.

You are not interpreting. You are describing location and timing, which is a factual report, and you are asking for the one thing you need: eyes on the paper.

## When it turns out to be a mimic

Sometimes the activation is cancelled because the elevation was early repolarization or pericarditis. That is not a failure, and it is not a reason to move slower next time. A department whose techs bring every chest pain tracing to a provider within minutes is a department where the real ones are caught.

> **On shift:** The single most common preventable delay in a chest pain workup is a tracing that was acquired on time and then sat somewhere for eleven minutes. Acquisition is half the job. Delivery is the other half.
keyPoints: Targets: 12-lead in a provider's hands under 10 minutes, door to balloon 90 minutes, 120 minutes with transfer and a 30-minute door-in-door-out.
On activation: repeat the tracing, pads and monitor on, two large-bore lines with the access wrist left free, labs with type and screen, metal off, nothing by mouth, route cleared.
Every tracing is labeled with name, second identifier, date, exact time and initials, plus any non-standard acquisition written by hand.
An unlabeled variation is worse than no tracing, because the difference will be read as a change in the patient.
Hand the tracing to a person and say who, what you saw, when, and what you want; never leave it on a counter or in a printer tray.

checks.q: What is the correct interpretation of the 10-minute door-to-ECG target?
choices: The tracing must be acquired within 10 minutes; delivery time is separate
The tracing must be acquired and in a provider's hands within 10 minutes
The patient must be in a bed within 10 minutes
The troponin must be drawn within 10 minutes
checks.why: A tracing sitting in a printer tray has not been interpreted, and the most common preventable delay is exactly that gap. Bed placement and laboratory draws have their own timelines and do not define this target.

checks.q: A code STEMI is called and you are starting an intravenous line. What should you confirm first?
choices: Whether the patient prefers the left or right arm
Which wrist and forearm the catheterization team wants left free for radial access
Whether the patient has had contrast before
Whether the lab prefers a green or gold tube
checks.why: Radial access requires an unpunctured wrist and forearm on the side the team plans to use, and a misplaced line can force a different access route. Patient preference, prior contrast and tube color do not change the access plan.

checks.q: You had to move the limb electrodes to the torso because of tremor. What must appear on the tracing?
choices: Nothing; the machine detects electrode position
A note that limb leads are on the torso and why, written on the paper
Only the filter setting used
A request that the tracing be repeated later
checks.why: Torso placement shifts the electrical axis and can create or erase findings, so an unlabeled tracing compared with a standard one shows a change that is pure geometry. Machines cannot detect electrode position, and the filter alone does not explain the altered morphology.

cards.front: What is sinus arrhythmia, and what is the first action?
cards.back: Normal beats whose R-to-R spacing varies with breathing, faster on inspiration. It is a normal variant common in the young. First action: none. Recognize it so you do not escalate it.

cards.front: How do you recognize a premature atrial contraction, and why does the count matter?
cards.back: An early beat with an oddly shaped or hidden P wave, a narrow normal QRS, and usually an incomplete pause. Frequent PACs predict atrial fibrillation, so report how many.

cards.front: What is a pulse deficit and when do you look for one?
cards.back: The gap between the monitor rate and the palpated rate in fast atrial fibrillation, caused by beats too weak to open the aortic valve. Report both numbers plus the blood pressure.

cards.front: Why is a narrow regular rhythm at exactly 150 suspicious?
cards.back: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction: the atria fire near 300 and the ventricles answer every other beat. Look for sawtooth waves in the inferior leads and V1 before calling it sinus tachycardia.

cards.front: How do you distinguish multifocal atrial tachycardia from atrial fibrillation?
cards.back: Both are irregularly irregular and fast, but MAT has P waves of at least three different shapes with varying PR intervals. Classic in severe COPD. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves at all.

cards.front: What defines a junctional rhythm, and what do you check?
cards.back: Regular, narrow, 40 to 60, with no P wave, an inverted P just before the QRS, or a P hidden after it. Check blood pressure, symptoms, and for digoxin, beta blockers or calcium channel blockers.

cards.front: What is the shared first action across every rhythm on the monitor?
cards.back: Touch the patient. The screen ranks possibilities; the pulse and the blood pressure decide urgency. No rhythm is reported without a matching look at the human.

cards.front: Name the PVC patterns and which one is most dangerous.
cards.back: Bigeminy is every other beat, trigeminy every third, a couplet is two in a row, three or more is a run of VT. R-on-T, where a PVC lands on the previous T wave, can trigger a lethal rhythm.

cards.front: How do you handle a wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin?
cards.back: Treat it as ventricular tachycardia. Feel a pulse, look at the patient, call the nurse, place defibrillator pads, bring the cart. In adults with heart disease it is VT most of the time.

cards.front: What does torsades de pointes look like, and what causes it?
cards.back: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that appears to twist around the baseline, complexes growing and shrinking. It arises from a long QT caused by drugs, low potassium or low magnesium. Magnesium is the treatment.

cards.front: Distinguish idioventricular from accelerated idioventricular rhythm.
cards.back: Both are wide with no P waves. Idioventricular runs 20 to 40 and is often agonal. Accelerated idioventricular runs 40 to 100 and commonly appears, usually benignly, just after a blocked artery reopens.

cards.front: Distinguish second-degree AV block type I from type II.
cards.back: Type I, Wenckebach: the PR interval stretches each beat until one QRS drops, then the cycle restarts. Type II: the PR stays constant and a QRS drops without warning. Type II is the dangerous one.

cards.front: How do you recognize third-degree heart block?
cards.back: P waves march at their own rate, QRS complexes march at theirs, with no relationship between them. Ventricular rate is usually 20 to 40 and the patient is often gray. Pulse, pressure, nurse, pads on.

cards.front: What are failure to capture and failure to sense on a paced strip?
cards.back: Failure to capture is a pacer spike with no QRS after it. Failure to sense is spikes appearing at random, including on T waves. Report the specific failure in plain words.

cards.front: What is the tech's role with a possible STEMI mimic?
cards.back: Never to adjudicate. Remove every artificial cause of abnormality, then move the tracing to a provider fast, every time. Describe what you see; do not name a diagnosis.

cards.front: How does benign early repolarization look?
cards.back: Concave upward ST elevation of 1 to 3 mm, most obvious in V2 to V5, with a notched or slurred J point and tall T waves. No reciprocal depression, and identical on prior tracings. Typically young patients.

cards.front: What distinguishes pericarditis from a STEMI on the tracing?
cards.back: Pericarditis shows diffuse concave elevation across multiple lead groups with PR segment depression and PR elevation in aVR, and no reciprocal depression. A STEMI respects one artery's territory.

cards.front: Why do left bundle branch block and paced rhythms mimic a STEMI?
cards.back: Both widen the QRS and produce ST segments that normally point opposite the main QRS direction, which looks like elevation. Sgarbossa criteria address when elevation in a wide-QRS tracing is real.

cards.front: What ECG progression does hyperkalemia produce?
cards.back: Tall narrow peaked T waves, then a flattened or absent P wave, then a widening QRS, then a sine wave. It mimics ischemia and is itself an emergency.

cards.front: Name four real ECG findings that are easy to miss.
cards.back: Hyperacute broad symmetric T waves, the Wellens pattern of deep T inversions in V2 and V3 while pain free, de Winter upsloping depression with tall T waves, and aVR elevation with widespread depression.

cards.front: What self-check comes before handing over a tracing with apparent ST elevation?
cards.back: Count the ribs, confirm a full-height calibration pulse, confirm 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV, confirm the diagnostic filter, and confirm limb electrodes are on limbs.

cards.front: Artifact appears only in leads III and aVF. Which electrode?
cards.back: The left leg electrode, since those two leads depend on it most. Dry the skin, use a fresh electrode from a sealed pack, press the edges, and drape the cable slack.

cards.front: The monitor alarms VTACH on a patient brushing his teeth. What do you do?
cards.back: Confirm a pulse, ask him to pause for ten seconds, and watch the baseline return. Reset the alarm and tell the nurse you checked it. A checked, documented alarm is not a nuisance alarm.

cards.front: All V leads are small with poor R wave progression. Likely cause?
cards.back: Electrodes placed on top of breast tissue, or dried gel. Tissue between electrode and heart attenuates the signal. Place V3 through V6 under the breast against the chest wall with fresh electrodes.

cards.front: Lead II is flat but leads I and III are normal and the patient has a pulse. What happened?
cards.back: Right arm and right leg electrodes reversed. Lead II compares RA to LL, and swapping in the ground reference collapses it. Check the colors, correct, repeat. Never chart it as asystole.

cards.front: The machine reads atrial fibrillation on a Parkinson patient with regular R-to-R intervals. What is it?
cards.back: Tremor artifact misread by the algorithm. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular, so regular spacing disproves it. Warm the patient, support the arms, and if needed move limb electrodes proximally and label it.

cards.front: State the four-step artifact troubleshooting method.
cards.back: Which leads are affected, one electrode or everything. Does the artifact have a pulse. What changed in the room in the last five minutes. Fix the physical cause, repeat, and label anything non-standard.

cards.front: What placement difference is common on pediatric ECGs?
cards.back: V4R is recorded in place of V3, or added to the standard twelve, because the right ventricle is a larger share of a child's heart. V4R is the 5th intercostal space, right midclavicular line. Label it.

cards.front: Why does a newborn have right axis deviation?
cards.back: In fetal circulation the right ventricle does most of the work, so it is the dominant chamber at birth. The axis migrates leftward over the first months as the left ventricle takes over.

cards.front: What is the juvenile T wave pattern?
cards.back: T wave inversion in V1 to V3, normal from about the first week of life through adolescence and sometimes into young adulthood. In young children an upright T wave in V1 is the abnormal finding.

cards.front: What are normal infant PR and QRS durations?
cards.back: PR roughly 0.08 to 0.12 s and QRS under about 0.08 s. Applying the adult cutoffs of 0.12 to 0.20 s and 0.12 s will wrongly flag normal children as abnormal.

cards.front: How do you distinguish sinus tachycardia from SVT in a child?
cards.back: Sinus tachycardia has P waves, varies with activity and fever, and usually stays under 220 in infants and 180 in children. SVT is fixed and metronomic with absent or abnormal P waves and faster rates.

cards.front: Which two pediatric ECG findings make a provider move?
cards.back: A short PR with a delta wave, suggesting Wolff-Parkinson-White, and a long corrected QT, screened for after exertional syncope, seizures, or a family history of sudden death or drowning.

cards.front: How do you get a clean tracing on a frightened child?
cards.back: Warm room and hands, parent close, demonstrate an electrode on yourself first, place everything before pressing record, then record during a quiet ten seconds. Remove electrodes slowly with adhesive remover.

cards.front: How does a posterior infarct appear on a standard 12-lead?
cards.back: As a mirror image in V1 to V3: ST depression instead of elevation, tall wide R waves instead of deep S waves, and upright prominent T waves. It is frequently mislabeled as ischemia.

cards.front: Where do V7, V8 and V9 go, and how do most machines record them?
cards.back: All at the V6 horizontal level: V7 posterior axillary line, V8 tip of the left scapula, V9 beside the spine. Most machines have six chest cables, so move V4 to V6 there and hand-relabel the tracing.

cards.front: What elevation threshold applies to posterior and right-sided leads?
cards.back: 0.5 mm, lower than the 1 mm in two contiguous standard leads, because the signal crosses more tissue to reach those positions.

cards.front: Why does an inferior STEMI trigger a right-sided tracing?
cards.back: The culprit is usually the right coronary artery, and roughly 40 percent of inferior infarcts involve the right ventricle, which changes treatment.

cards.front: Why is nitroglycerin dangerous in a right ventricular infarct?
cards.back: A damaged right ventricle cannot generate pressure on its own and depends on filling. Nitroglycerin drops preload and can cause profound hypotension. Fluid is the treatment instead.

cards.front: What happens if a right-sided tracing is not labeled?
cards.back: The next reader sees a pattern that looks like dextrocardia, and comparing it to the previous standard tracing manufactures a dramatic change that is pure geometry.

cards.front: Does an extra-lead tracing replace the standard 12-lead?
cards.back: No. It supplements it. Both go in the chart, both are timed and initialed, and the standard tracing remains the comparison for everything that follows.

cards.front: What three settings does every tracing print in the footer, and why read them first?
cards.back: Paper speed, gain and filter settings. All three change the shape of the waveform, so a tracing cannot be compared or interpreted until you know which were used.

cards.front: What do half standard and double standard gain do?
cards.back: Half standard, 5 mm/mV, keeps very tall complexes from overlapping but halves every ST deviation on the page. Double standard, 20 mm/mV, enlarges small complexes and doubles apparent ST change.

cards.front: How do you know which gain a tracing used?
cards.back: The calibration pulse. A full-height rectangular pulse ten small boxes tall means standard 10 mm/mV; half height means half standard. It takes one second to check and it changes everything.

cards.front: What are the three ECG filters and their diagnostic settings?
cards.back: Low-pass high-frequency cutoff at 150 Hz for adults and 250 Hz for children; high-pass low-frequency cutoff at 0.05 Hz; notch AC filter at 60 Hz in the United States.

cards.front: What does monitor-mode filtering do to a diagnostic tracing?
cards.back: A 40 Hz low-pass shaves QRS detail and can attenuate ST segments; a 0.5 Hz high-pass distorts the ST segment, producing artificial depression or elevation. Monitor mode is not a diagnostic tracing.

cards.front: Why must the patient's real age and sex be entered into the machine?
cards.back: Interpretive algorithms use sex- and age-specific thresholds, including V2 and V3 elevation criteria of 2 mm in men 40 and over, 2.5 mm in men under 40, and 1.5 mm in women.

cards.front: Why does an ectopic beat appear in only one column of the printout?
cards.back: All twelve leads are acquired simultaneously over about 10 seconds but printed in four columns of 2.5 seconds, so a beat shows only in the column covering its moment. The rhythm strip is the continuous record.

cards.front: How often are serial ECGs repeated, and what else triggers one?
cards.back: Every 15 to 30 minutes during ongoing chest pain, and immediately on any change in pain, vital signs, rhythm, or anything the patient says is different.

cards.front: Why write the pain score on each tracing?
cards.back: So the clinician can pair the picture with the symptom. A pain-free tracing and a painful one mean different things, and the Wellens pattern specifically appears during pain-free intervals.

cards.front: State the usual troponin timing for high-sensitivity and conventional assays.
cards.back: High-sensitivity at 0 and 1 hour, or 0 and 2 or 3 hours by protocol. Conventional at 0, 3 and 6 hours. The delta between values matters more than a single number.

cards.front: Why does a troponin drawn 40 minutes late break the algorithm?
cards.back: Rule-in and rule-out pathways compare values across a defined interval, so a late sample is not a one-hour value and cannot be interpreted against the threshold. Draw on time and label the exact time.

cards.front: A patient's ECG is unchanged but troponin goes from 55 to 240 in an hour. What does that mean?
cards.back: A rising delta with a normal ECG indicates a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The ECG is not the only clock, and this patient is admitted for catheterization on a slower timeline.

cards.front: What changes when a chest pain patient has a paced rhythm?
cards.back: Pacing distorts ST segments, so the tracing is less reliable and serial troponin carries more weight. Keep repeating tracings anyway, and say out loud that the patient is paced.

cards.front: State the STEMI system timeline from arrival to intervention.
cards.back: 12-lead in a provider's hands under 10 minutes, catheterization team in house in 20 to 30 minutes, door to balloon 90 minutes, 120 minutes if transfer is needed with a 30-minute door-in-door-out, thrombolytics within 30 minutes if no lab.

cards.front: List the tech's tasks the moment a code STEMI is called.
cards.back: Repeat the 12-lead, pads and monitor on, full vitals, two large-bore IVs with the access wrist left free, labs with type and screen, metal and clothing off, nothing by mouth, bed and route ready, tracings travel with the patient.

cards.front: Which arm should be left free during a STEMI activation, and why?
cards.back: Whichever wrist and forearm the catheterization team plans to use for radial access. Ask. A misplaced line can force them to a different access route.

cards.front: What non-standard details get hand-written on a tracing?
cards.back: Right-sided or posterior with lead relabeling, limb leads on torso and why, any filter or gain change and why, non-supine position, oxygen device and flow, and the pain score at acquisition.

cards.front: Give the four-part ECG handoff sentence.
cards.back: Who, what you saw, when, and what you want. For example: bed 4, the 58-year-old with chest pressure, this tracing is two minutes old, elevation in two, three and aVF, can you look now.

cards.front: A STEMI activation is cancelled because the tracing was a mimic. What does that mean for next time?
cards.back: Nothing changes. A department whose techs bring every chest pain tracing to a provider within minutes is the department that catches the real ones. Speed of delivery is the standard, not the diagnosis.

quiz.q: A monitored patient's rhythm is narrow and upright-P with R-to-R intervals that lengthen and shorten in time with respiration. He is asymptomatic. What is the correct action?
choices: Recognize sinus arrhythmia, a normal variant, and take no action
Report it as a new irregular rhythm and obtain a 12-lead immediately
Treat it as atrial fibrillation until a 12-lead proves otherwise
Replace all monitoring electrodes to eliminate artifact
quiz.why: Respiratory variation with normal upright P waves is sinus arrhythmia, a normal finding especially in young patients. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves, and the pattern is physiologic rather than an electrode problem.

quiz.q: The monitor shows atrial fibrillation at 152 while you count a radial pulse of 98. The patient is pale. What do you report?
choices: That the monitor is in error and the true rate is 98
That the oximeter probe needs repositioning
Both rates and the blood pressure, because a pulse deficit means not every beat is perfusing
That the patient has converted to sinus rhythm
quiz.why: Short filling times in rapid atrial fibrillation leave some beats without enough stroke volume to reach the wrist, and the gap itself is the clinical finding. Neither rate is an error, and no conversion has occurred.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with COPD has an irregularly irregular rhythm at 118. Looking closely, P waves are present with at least three different shapes and varying PR intervals. What is this?
choices: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Atrial flutter with variable conduction
Sinus tachycardia with premature ventricular contractions
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
quiz.why: Three or more P wave morphologies with varying PR intervals at a rate over 100 defines multifocal atrial tachycardia, classically in severe lung disease. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves, flutter shows sawtooth waves, and PVCs are wide.

quiz.q: A patient's strip is narrow, regular, at 46, with no visible P waves. His blood pressure is 96/58 and he feels lightheaded. What should you do first?
choices: Document a junctional rhythm and continue rounding
Increase the monitor gain to look for P waves before telling anyone
Ask him to cough repeatedly to raise his rate
Tell the nurse now with the rate, the pressure, the symptom, and ask about rate-slowing medications
quiz.why: A junctional escape rhythm with symptoms and a borderline pressure needs immediate escalation, and medication history frequently explains it. Charting without reporting, hunting for P waves first, or improvising a vagal maneuver all delay care.

quiz.q: A chest pain patient's monitor shows two wide bizarre beats in a row, then normal beats, then another wide beat landing on the previous T wave. What do you report?
choices: Artifact from a loose electrode
A couplet plus an R-on-T beat, reported to the nurse immediately with the frequency
Bigeminy, which is benign and needs no report
A run of ventricular tachycardia requiring immediate defibrillation
quiz.why: Two in a row is a couplet, and a PVC landing on a T wave can trigger a lethal rhythm, so both belong in an immediate report. Bigeminy is every other beat, three or more in a row defines a run, and defibrillation applies to pulseless rhythms.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with a prior infarct develops a wide regular tachycardia at 168 with a weak pulse and a blood pressure of 88/50. What is the correct action?
choices: Assume supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy and reassure him
Leave to find a 12-lead machine before alerting anyone
Stay with the patient, call the nurse, place defibrillator pads and bring the cart
Check all electrodes first, since wide complexes are usually artifact
quiz.why: A wide regular tachycardia in an adult with structural heart disease is ventricular tachycardia most of the time, and hypotension makes it unstable. Assuming aberrancy, leaving the room, or delaying for an electrode check all risk an arrest with nobody present.

quiz.q: A strip shows polymorphic wide complexes that grow taller then shorter in a twisting pattern. The patient is on a medication known to prolong the QT. What is this and what is the specific treatment?
choices: Ventricular fibrillation, treated with immediate defibrillation only
Torsades de pointes, with magnesium as the specific treatment
Atrial flutter with aberrancy, treated with rate control
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm, which requires no treatment
quiz.why: The twisting polymorphic pattern arising from a long QT is torsades de pointes, and magnesium is the specific therapy alongside standard resuscitation if pulseless. Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic without the twisting envelope, and the other options are neither polymorphic nor QT related.

quiz.q: On a rhythm strip the PR interval is identical on every conducted beat, and then a P wave appears with no QRS after it, without any warning. What is this and why does it matter?
choices: Second-degree type II block, which can progress to complete block and often needs pacing
Wenckebach, which is usually benign
First-degree block, which requires no action
Sinus arrest with a junctional escape
quiz.why: A constant PR with an abruptly dropped QRS is type II block, which is unstable and frequently leads to pacing. Wenckebach lengthens the PR progressively, first-degree block drops nothing, and sinus arrest shows an absent P wave rather than a blocked one.

quiz.q: A 27-year-old athlete with pleuritic chest pain has concave ST elevation in six leads spanning more than one territory, with PR segment depression and PR elevation in aVR. What pattern does this describe?
choices: Acute pericarditis
Anterior STEMI with reciprocal change
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hyperkalemia
quiz.why: Diffuse concave elevation crossing arterial territories with PR depression and PR elevation in aVR is the pericarditis pattern. A STEMI respects one artery's territory and produces reciprocal depression, hypertrophy produces high voltage with lateral strain, and hyperkalemia peaks T waves.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old is currently pain free after two earlier episodes of chest pressure. His tracing shows deep symmetric T wave inversions in V2 and V3. What should you do?
choices: File it as a normal variant since he is asymptomatic
Hand it to a provider now and state that he is pain free and this pattern is new
Repeat the tracing only if the pain returns
Move V2 and V3 lower and reprint, since the inversion is likely misplacement
quiz.why: The Wellens pattern signals a critically narrowed left anterior descending artery and typically appears during the pain-free window, so the pain-free state is part of the report rather than reassurance. High V1 and V2 placement inverts P waves rather than producing deep symmetric T inversions.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient has tall narrow peaked T waves, a barely visible P wave, and a QRS that looks wider than his prior tracing. What should you do?
choices: Treat it as a benign variant since there is no ST elevation
Get the tracing to a provider immediately, since this progression suggests hyperkalemia
Change to the 40 Hz filter to sharpen the T waves
Reprint at double gain to measure the T waves accurately
