quiz.why: Peaked T waves with a vanishing P wave and a widening QRS is the hyperkalemia progression, which precedes a sine wave and arrest. Filtering and gain changes alter appearance without addressing an electrolyte emergency.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a tech's role when a tracing may represent a STEMI mimic?
choices: Decide whether it is a mimic before disturbing a provider
Remove artificial causes of abnormality, then deliver it to a provider immediately regardless
Wait for the serial tracing to clarify the pattern
Ask another tech for a second opinion first
quiz.why: Adjudication belongs to a licensed clinician, and the tech's leverage is eliminating misplacement, wrong calibration and filter errors that manufacture false alarms. Waiting or polling colleagues adds delay without adding diagnostic value.

quiz.q: A 12-lead shows fuzzy drifting baseline in leads III and aVF only. Every other lead is clean. What is the fix?
choices: Replace the right arm electrode
Replace the left leg electrode and dry the skin under it
Replace all six chest electrodes
Switch to the 40 Hz filter and reprint
quiz.why: III and aVF are the leads most dependent on the left leg electrode, so isolated artifact there localizes to LL. A right arm problem would corrupt lead I and aVR, chest electrodes affect only V leads, and filtering hides the problem instead of fixing it.

quiz.q: A tracing on a woman with large breasts shows normal limb leads but very small V leads with almost no R wave progression. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Chest electrodes placed on top of breast tissue rather than against the chest wall
An anterior infarct with loss of R waves
The gain was set to double standard
Right arm and left arm electrode reversal
quiz.why: Tissue between the electrode and the heart attenuates the precordial signal and fakes poor R wave progression, which is why V3 through V6 go under the breast. Double gain would enlarge rather than shrink complexes, and limb reversal does not affect chest leads.

quiz.q: A clean tracing at 0200 is followed at 0215 by one with a perfectly regular fuzzy thickening in every lead. A forced-air warming blanket was started in between. What is the correct first response?
choices: Apply the notch filter and accept the tracing
Replace all ten electrodes
Document 60-cycle interference and do not repeat the tracing
Move or unplug the device, separate the cable from power cords, untangle the wires, then repeat
quiz.why: Regular high-frequency fuzz across every lead is alternating-current interference, and the physical source is the fix. Filtering first hides evidence and can hide real ST findings, electrodes are not the problem, and leaving an uninterpretable tracing in the chart helps nobody.

quiz.q: The interpretive statement reads ATRIAL FIBRILLATION, but the R-to-R intervals on the strip are perfectly regular and the patient has a resting tremor. What is happening?
choices: The patient has atrial fibrillation with a regularized ventricular response
The paper speed was set to 50 mm/s
The chest electrodes were placed too low
Tremor artifact is producing fibrillatory-looking baseline that the algorithm misread
quiz.why: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular by definition, so perfectly regular spacing disproves it and points at fine tremor artifact deceiving the algorithm. Paper speed and chest electrode position change appearance in other specific ways.

quiz.q: An 11-year-old's ECG shows T wave inversion in V1 through V3 and no other abnormality. He is here for a sprained wrist. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The juvenile T wave pattern, which is normal at this age
Anterior ischemia requiring urgent evaluation
Evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy
Proof that V1 and V2 were placed in the second intercostal space
quiz.why: Right precordial T wave inversion is normal from infancy through adolescence and often into young adulthood. High V1 and V2 placement inverts P waves, and this finding alone establishes neither ischemia nor hypertrophy.

quiz.q: A 5-month-old has a narrow rhythm at 244 that has not varied at all, with no discernible P waves. He is fussy but perfusing. What does this favor and what do you do?
choices: Sinus tachycardia from fever; continue routine triage
Normal infant heart rate; no action needed
Supraventricular tachycardia; tell the nurse immediately and stay with the infant
Artifact from crying; repeat the tracing when he settles
quiz.why: A fixed rate above 220 in an infant with absent P waves favors supraventricular tachycardia, since sinus tachycardia varies with state and rarely exceeds 220. Crying artifact distorts the baseline rather than producing regular narrow complexes at a metronomic rate.

quiz.q: An infant's tracing shows a PR interval of 0.10 s and a QRS of 0.07 s. How should these be read?
choices: Short PR suggesting a bypass tract, with a narrow QRS
First-degree block with an incomplete bundle branch block
Normal for an infant, since intervals are shorter at this age
Evidence the paper speed was set to 50 mm/s
quiz.why: Infant PR intervals run roughly 0.08 to 0.12 s and QRS durations under about 0.08 s, so both values are normal for the age. Applying adult cutoffs is exactly how normal children get falsely flagged, and a bypass tract also requires a delta wave.

quiz.q: You need a 12-lead on a frightened 4-year-old. Which approach is most likely to produce a readable tracing?
choices: Have two staff hold the child still and record immediately
Warm the room, keep a parent close, demonstrate an electrode on yourself, place everything, then record during a quiet ten seconds
Sedate the child before attempting the tracing
Record three tracings quickly and choose the cleanest
quiz.why: A struggling child produces unreadable tracings and loses trust for everything afterward, so the technique is to prepare fully and wait for ten quiet seconds. Restraint worsens artifact, sedation is never a tech decision, and repeated fast attempts do not fix the underlying motion.

quiz.q: A chest pain tracing shows 2 mm of ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall broad R waves and upright T waves. What is the likely significance?
choices: Non-specific ischemia that can be worked up on a routine timeline
Right ventricular infarct requiring V4R
Digoxin effect
A posterior infarct seen in mirror image, which needs posterior leads and urgent attention
quiz.why: Depression with tall R waves in the right precordial leads is the front-facing mirror of posterior elevation, so it represents a completely occluded artery and needs V7 to V9. Right-sided leads follow inferior elevation, and digoxin produces a sagging ST rather than tall R waves.

quiz.q: Where do V7, V8 and V9 belong?
choices: At the 5th intercostal space on the right chest
One intercostal space below V4, V5 and V6
Along the sternum at the 2nd, 3rd and 4th intercostal spaces
All at the V6 horizontal level: posterior axillary line, tip of the left scapula, and beside the spine
quiz.why: The posterior leads wrap around the left side at V6's horizontal level, which is why they are usually recorded by moving V4 to V6 and relabeling. The right chest position is V4R territory, and neither a lower rib space nor a sternal line describes posterior leads.

quiz.q: An inferior STEMI is confirmed and V4R shows 0.5 mm of ST elevation. The nurse is about to give nitroglycerin. What is the concern?
choices: Nitroglycerin will worsen the ST elevation on the tracing
V4R elevation means the tracing was taken with reversed arm leads
0.5 mm is below the diagnostic threshold and can be ignored
Right ventricular involvement is preload dependent, so nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension
quiz.why: A damaged right ventricle depends on filling, so a vasodilator that drops preload can collapse cardiac output, and fluid is the treatment instead. The posterior and right-sided threshold is 0.5 mm precisely because the signal crosses more tissue.

quiz.q: You obtain a right-sided tracing and forget to label it. What is the likely consequence?
choices: None, since the machine records electrode positions automatically
The tracing will be rejected by the laboratory
The next reader may interpret it as dextrocardia or as a dramatic change from the previous standard tracing
The interpretive algorithm will refuse to print a statement
quiz.why: Machines have no way to detect moved electrodes, so unlabeled right-sided leads look like a global abnormality and manufacture a change that is pure geometry. Tracings are not processed by a laboratory and the algorithm will still print its usual statement.

quiz.q: The calibration pulse on a chest pain tracing is half height. The tracing shows 1 mm of ST elevation in V3 and V4. What does this mean?
choices: The elevation is exaggerated and is really 0.5 mm
The machine is at half standard gain, so the true elevation is about 2 mm
The paper speed was 50 mm/s
The tracing is unusable and must be discarded without comment
quiz.why: Half standard gain of 5 mm/mV halves every amplitude on the page, so printed elevation represents twice as much real voltage. Paper speed affects horizontal width, and the tracing is usable once the calibration is recognized and noted.

quiz.q: Which filter configuration is correct for a diagnostic adult 12-lead?
choices: High-pass 0.05 Hz and low-pass 150 Hz
High-pass 0.5 Hz and low-pass 40 Hz
High-pass 0.05 Hz and low-pass 40 Hz
High-pass 0.5 Hz and low-pass 250 Hz
quiz.why: Diagnostic mode for adults is 0.05 to 150 Hz; children use an upper cutoff up to 250 Hz. A 0.5 Hz high-pass distorts the ST segment and a 40 Hz low-pass attenuates real ST and QRS detail, which is why both are monitor-mode settings.

quiz.q: A tracing on a 38-year-old woman was recorded with the machine's default demographics of a 50-year-old male. Why does this matter?
choices: It only affects how the tracing is filed in the chart
It changes the paper speed to 50 mm/s
The interpretive algorithm applies sex- and age-specific thresholds, so the printed conclusion can change
It disables the pacemaker spike detection
quiz.why: The V2 and V3 elevation criteria differ by sex and age, so wrong demographics apply the wrong cutoff to a real decision. Filing errors also matter, but speed and spike detection are set independently of demographics.

quiz.q: At the start of your shift, which ECG machine check has the largest effect on time-based quality measures?
choices: Wiping the cables with disinfectant
Confirming the machine's date and time are set correctly
Counting the remaining electrode packs
Verifying the screen brightness
quiz.why: A wrong clock corrupts every door-to-ECG measurement and every serial comparison, which are the metrics the chest pain pathway runs on. Cleaning, supplies and display settings matter operationally but do not alter timestamps.

quiz.q: A chest pain patient's first tracing is normal. Twenty-five minutes later his pain is unchanged at 7 out of 10 and the first troponin has not resulted. What should happen?
choices: Repeat the 12-lead now, because roughly a third of infarcts are normal on the first tracing
Wait for the troponin before repeating a tracing
Repeat only if the pain increases
Rely on continuous monitoring instead
quiz.why: Serial tracings every 15 to 30 minutes during ongoing pain are the standard, and a dynamic change often appears before the troponin rises. Waiting on a laboratory value, requiring worsening pain, or substituting telemetry all delay a finding a repeat would catch.

quiz.q: A high-sensitivity troponin protocol requires a repeat at one hour. Because of a trauma activation, the second tube is drawn at 1 hour and 40 minutes. What is the consequence?
choices: The value cannot be interpreted as a one-hour result and the algorithm cannot be applied as written
No consequence; troponin rises steadily so any interval works
The specimen will hemolyze because of the delay
The laboratory will apply a different reference range automatically
quiz.why: Rule-in and rule-out pathways compare values across a defined interval, so an off-schedule draw breaks the algorithm even if the number is accurate. Delay does not cause hemolysis, and laboratories do not silently change reference ranges based on timing.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old's three serial tracings are identical and unremarkable, but his troponin rises from 48 to 210 over one hour. What does this indicate?
choices: A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, since the rising delta is diagnostic even with an unchanged ECG
A laboratory error requiring a redraw before anyone is told
Chronic troponin elevation from kidney disease
That the tracings were recorded in monitor mode
quiz.why: A significant rise between timed values indicates acute myocardial injury regardless of a normal ECG. Chronic elevation is characterized by a stable value without a delta, and a rising pattern is not explained by filter settings.

quiz.q: Why should the pain score be written on each serial tracing?
choices: For billing documentation only
Because the machine requires it to print an interpretation
So the clinician can pair the electrical picture with the symptom at that moment
To determine which filter to use
quiz.why: The same tracing means different things during pain and during a pain-free interval, which is exactly why the Wellens pattern is defined by appearing while pain free. Billing, machine function and filter selection are unrelated.

quiz.q: A code STEMI is called on a patient who will likely go for radial access. You are starting the second intravenous line. What should you confirm?
choices: Whether the patient has a preferred arm
Whether the patient has ever had contrast
Which tube color the laboratory prefers
Which wrist and forearm the catheterization team wants left unpunctured
quiz.why: Radial access requires an unpunctured wrist and forearm on the planned side, and a misplaced line can force a different access route and cost time. Preference, prior contrast and tube color do not affect the access plan.

quiz.q: You acquire a chest pain tracing in triage at 7 minutes after arrival, then place it in the printer tray while you room another patient. A provider sees it 14 minutes later. Was the target met?
choices: Yes, because acquisition occurred within 10 minutes
Yes, because 21 minutes is within the 90-minute window
No, because the target is the tracing in a provider's hands within 10 minutes
It cannot be determined without the troponin result
quiz.why: A tracing nobody has read has not been interpreted, and this exact gap is the most common preventable delay in a chest pain workup. The 90-minute figure is door to balloon, a downstream measure that this delay directly threatens.

quiz.q: Which handoff statement is appropriate from a tech delivering a tracing?
choices: This patient is having an inferior STEMI and needs the cath lab
The machine says acute MI suspected, so I activated the cath lab
Bed 4, the 58-year-old with chest pressure, this tracing is two minutes old, there is elevation in two, three and aVF, can you look now
I left it in the rack if you get a chance
quiz.why: Describing location and timing and asking for eyes on the paper is factual reporting within scope. Naming a diagnosis or activating a team exceeds the role, and leaving a tracing in a rack is the delay the whole protocol exists to prevent.

scenarios.title: The machine says ACUTE MI on a 24-year-old
scenarios.intro: A 24-year-old man walks into triage with three days of sharp left-sided chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and better when he leans forward. He had a bad cold last week. He is not diaphoretic. The triage nurse asks you to get a 12-lead under the chest pain standing order.

steps.prompt: You get the machine. He is thin, with a hairy chest and a small tattoo across the left upper chest. What do you do about placement?

choices.text: Find the sternal angle, count to the 4th intercostal space, clip a patch of hair only where each electrode goes, and place normally over the tattoo.
choices.feedback: Correct. Tattooed skin conducts normally. Clip only what you need and count bone rather than guessing from the nipple line.

choices.text: Shift V1 and V2 up one space to avoid the tattoo.
choices.feedback: Never move a lead for cosmetic reasons. V1 and V2 placed too high produce an rSr pattern, inverted P waves and pseudo-anterior ST changes, which is exactly the false alarm you are trying to avoid.

choices.text: Shave the whole chest so the electrodes stick well.
choices.feedback: Clip, never shave. A razor causes micro-cuts in a patient who may receive blood thinners within the hour, and you only need a patch under each electrode.

steps.prompt: The tracing prints. Across the top the machine states `ACUTE MI SUSPECTED`. You see concave ST elevation in leads I, II, aVF, V3, V4, V5 and V6, with PR segment depression in several leads and PR elevation in aVR. There is no depression in I or aVL.

choices.text: Check the calibration pulse and settings, then hand the tracing to a provider immediately and describe what you see.
choices.feedback: Correct. Rule out your own contribution in one second, then deliver. Every chest pain tracing goes to a provider fast, whatever you think it shows.

choices.text: Recognize a pericarditis pattern and put the tracing in the chart rack for the provider to find.
choices.feedback: Even a correct suspicion does not change the delivery rule. Racks and counters are where tracings go to sit for eleven minutes.

choices.text: Repeat the tracing first to see whether the pattern persists.
choices.feedback: Serial tracings are valuable, but the first one still goes to a provider now. Repeat after, not instead.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse to activate the cath lab because the machine says acute MI.
choices.feedback: Activation is a provider decision. The machine's statement is a hint that misses real infarcts and invents others.

steps.prompt: The physician looks at it and says: diffuse, concave, PR depression, no reciprocal change, young patient with positional pleuritic pain after a viral illness. She is thinking pericarditis but wants to be careful. She asks whether there is a prior tracing.

choices.text: Check for a prior ECG in the record and bring it, and mention he has no reciprocal depression in I or aVL.
choices.feedback: Correct. A prior tracing is the single most useful comparison, and reporting the absence of reciprocal change is description, not diagnosis.

choices.text: Tell her there is no prior because he is young.
choices.feedback: Assumption, not a check. Young patients have prior tracings from sports physicals, other visits and urgent care.

choices.text: Offer to do a right-sided tracing.
choices.feedback: Right-sided leads follow inferior ST elevation, and the pattern here spans multiple territories. Not wrong to offer, but not the right extra study.

steps.prompt: There is a prior tracing from two years ago that is completely normal. The physician orders troponins and a repeat ECG in 30 minutes, and does not activate the cath lab. A new tech asks you whether the machine was wrong.

choices.text: Explain that the software flags patterns and a person decides, and that the process worked because the tracing reached a provider in minutes.
choices.feedback: Correct. The measure of the system is delivery time, not whether the algorithm was right.

choices.text: Tell her the machine is usually wrong and can be ignored on young patients.
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Young patients have infarcts, and teaching anyone to discount a flagged tracing based on age creates the miss.

choices.text: Say you are not sure and to ask the physician.
choices.feedback: Safe but a missed teaching moment. You can explain the process without interpreting the tracing.

scenarios.debrief: Two rules held this case together. First, never move an electrode for convenience or cosmetics: V1 and V2 one space high is the single most reliable way to manufacture an anterior pseudo-infarct, and the tattoo, the chest hair and the tight rib spacing all tempt you toward it. Second, recognizing a mimic never changes what you do with the paper. Diffuse concave elevation crossing several arterial territories, PR segment depression, PR elevation in aVR, and no reciprocal change is a textbook pericarditis pattern, and it still goes into a provider's hand within seconds. Your leverage is removing artificial abnormality and shortening delivery time. A cancelled activation is not a failure; a tracing sitting in a rack is.

scenarios.title: ST depression in V1 to V3, and the lead you have not placed yet
scenarios.intro: A 61-year-old woman arrives with 90 minutes of chest pressure and nausea. She is pale. You get a 12-lead within 6 minutes of arrival. The provider is at the bedside of another patient two rooms away.

steps.prompt: The tracing shows `2 mm` of ST depression in V1, V2 and V3 with tall broad R waves and upright T waves in those leads. There is no ST elevation anywhere. What do you do with it?

choices.text: Take it to the provider now and describe it: depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves.
choices.feedback: Correct. That triad is the mirror image of posterior elevation and is frequently downgraded to ischemia. Description, delivered immediately, is exactly your role.

choices.text: Put it in the chart since there is no ST elevation.
choices.feedback: No elevation is precisely how a posterior occlusion gets missed. The standard twelve leads do not look at the back wall.

choices.text: Repeat the tracing to confirm the depression is real.
choices.feedback: A repeat is reasonable later, but this one goes to a provider now. She has had pressure for 90 minutes.

choices.text: Move V1 to V3 down one space to see whether the depression resolves.
choices.feedback: Never move electrodes to make a finding disappear. Confirm correct placement, then deliver the tracing.

steps.prompt: The provider looks and says: posterior until proven otherwise, get me posterior leads. Your machine has only six chest cables.

choices.text: Move V4, V5 and V6 to the V7, V8 and V9 positions, reprint, and hand-label `V4 = V7, V5 = V8, V6 = V9`.
choices.feedback: Correct. That is the standard workaround, and the hand label is what stops the next reader believing those are standard positions.

choices.text: Tell her posterior leads are not possible without a 15-lead machine.
choices.feedback: They are entirely possible by relocating three chest electrodes. This answer costs the patient the study.

choices.text: Add three extra electrodes to the back and hope the machine reads them.
choices.feedback: Electrodes without cables record nothing. You must move the cables to the new positions.

choices.text: Move V4, V5 and V6 to the back and reprint without labeling, then tell her verbally.
choices.feedback: The reprint is right but an unlabeled tracing in a chart outlives the verbal handoff and will be misread later.

steps.prompt: You need to place V7, V8 and V9. She is pale and uncomfortable but able to move with help.

choices.text: Get a second person, roll her toward you with the monitor still on, place all three at the V6 horizontal level, and roll her back or have her sit forward for the recording.
choices.feedback: Correct. Two people, monitor stays on, and all three leads at the V6 level: posterior axillary line, scapular tip, beside the spine.

choices.text: Sit her fully upright on the edge of the bed by herself and place them quickly.
choices.feedback: A pale patient with an active infarct can become syncopal sitting up unsupported. Use help and keep her monitored.

choices.text: Place them one intercostal space below V6 since the back sits lower.
choices.feedback: All three posterior leads sit at the same horizontal level as V6. Dropping a space puts them below the target region.

steps.prompt: The posterior tracing shows `0.8 mm` of ST elevation in the V8 position. The provider activates the cath lab.

choices.text: Understand that 0.5 mm is the diagnostic threshold posteriorly, and move to the activation task list.
choices.feedback: Correct. The threshold is lower because the signal crosses more tissue. Now pads, monitor, lines, labs, route.

choices.text: Question the activation, since 0.8 mm is under the usual 1 mm STEMI criterion.
choices.feedback: The 1 mm figure applies to standard leads. Posterior and right-sided leads use 0.5 mm precisely because the signal is attenuated.

choices.text: Repeat the posterior tracing to confirm before doing anything else.
choices.feedback: Confirmation has been made by the provider. Repeating now spends minutes of muscle.

steps.prompt: During activation, you are asked to get both tracings ready to travel with the patient.

choices.text: Send copies of the original standard 12-lead and the labeled posterior tracing, both timed and initialed, keeping copies for the chart.
choices.feedback: Correct. The extra tracing supplements, never replaces, and the cath team wants both.

choices.text: Send only the posterior tracing since it is the one that showed elevation.
choices.feedback: The standard tracing is the baseline everything is compared against, including anything recorded after the procedure.

choices.text: Send both but without the times, since the nurse will report them verbally.
choices.feedback: Every tracing carries name, second identifier, date, exact time and initials. Verbal times do not survive the handoff chain.

scenarios.debrief: This case is one pattern and one procedure. The pattern is the posterior mirror: ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall broad R waves and upright T waves in a chest pain patient means a completely blocked artery that the standard twelve leads cannot see, and calling it non-specific ischemia is the classic delay. The procedure is the electrode relocation: V4, V5 and V6 move to the posterior axillary line, the scapular tip and beside the spine, all at the V6 horizontal level, and the tracing is hand-labeled so nobody reads it as standard. Two numbers carry over to every extra-lead study you will ever do. Posterior and right-sided leads are diagnostic at 0.5 mm rather than 1 mm, and the supplementary tracing never replaces the original, which remains the comparison for everything that follows.

scenarios.title: Fifteen minutes later, everything changed
scenarios.intro: A 57-year-old man is in bed 6 with 50 minutes of chest pressure. You obtained a 12-lead at 4 minutes after arrival; it was read as normal sinus rhythm with no acute changes. The first troponin was drawn at the same time. He has been in the bed for 15 minutes and is still rating his pain 7 out of 10.

steps.prompt: You are passing bed 6 and he says the pressure is the same. What should you do?

choices.text: Repeat the 12-lead now, since he has ongoing pain and about a third of infarcts are normal on the first tracing.
choices.feedback: Correct. Serial tracings every 15 to 30 minutes during ongoing pain are the standard, and this is the interval.

choices.text: Wait for the troponin to result, then decide.
choices.feedback: The ECG often changes before the troponin rises. Waiting on the lab spends the window the repeat tracing exists to catch.

choices.text: Tell the nurse he still hurts and go back to your other tasks.
choices.feedback: Reporting is right but incomplete. The repeat tracing falls within your standing orders and should not wait behind a conversation.

steps.prompt: The repeat tracing shows `2.5 mm` of ST elevation in II, III and aVF with `1.5 mm` of depression in I and aVL. You write the time and his pain score on it.

choices.text: Take it directly to a provider and say: bed 6, repeat tracing one minute old, elevation in two, three and aVF with depression in one and aVL, pain still seven.
choices.feedback: Correct. Who, what you saw, when, what you want, all in one breath, and the reciprocal change is part of the description.

choices.text: Scan it into the chart and send a message to the provider.
choices.feedback: This is time-critical paper. It goes into a hand, not into a queue.

choices.text: Tell the nurse the machine did not print an acute statement so it is probably fine.
choices.feedback: The algorithm misses real infarcts routinely. What you described is an inferior STEMI pattern with reciprocal change.

choices.text: Get a third tracing to be sure before reporting.
choices.feedback: Confirming a finding by delaying it is the wrong trade. Report, then repeat if asked.

steps.prompt: A code STEMI is called. The provider says: get me a right-sided tracing before anyone gives nitroglycerin.

choices.text: Place V4R at the 5th intercostal space in the right midclavicular line, mirror the remaining positions, print, and label the tracing right-sided.
choices.feedback: Correct, and the label is essential or the next reader sees dextrocardia.

choices.text: Place V4R at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal border.
choices.feedback: That is the V1 position. V4R mirrors V4: 5th intercostal space, right midclavicular line.

choices.text: Tell the provider a right-sided tracing will delay transport.
choices.feedback: It takes about ninety seconds and it changes whether a drug is safe. This is not a delay worth objecting to.

steps.prompt: V4R shows `0.7 mm` of elevation. The provider holds the nitroglycerin and orders a fluid bolus instead. The nurse asks you to get two lines in.

choices.text: Ask which wrist the cath team wants left free, then place two large-bore lines accordingly.
choices.feedback: Correct. Radial access needs an unpunctured wrist and forearm on the planned side.

choices.text: Place both lines in the right antecubital fossa for speed.
choices.feedback: Fast, but it can block the access route the team intends to use. Ask first; it costs five seconds.

choices.text: Question the fluid order, since fluids seem wrong in a heart attack.
choices.feedback: A right ventricular infarct is preload dependent, so fluid is the correct treatment and nitroglycerin is the danger.

steps.prompt: The cath lab is ready. You are gathering what travels with him.

choices.text: Copies of the initial normal tracing, the repeat showing elevation, and the labeled right-sided tracing, all timed and initialed.
choices.feedback: Correct. The normal first tracing matters as much as the abnormal one, because it establishes when the change occurred.

choices.text: Only the tracing showing ST elevation, since that is the diagnostic one.
choices.feedback: Without the earlier normal tracing, nobody downstream can tell how recent the occlusion is.

choices.text: All three tracings, unlabeled, with a verbal summary to the transport nurse.
choices.feedback: Unlabeled tracings, particularly the right-sided one, will be misread once the verbal handoff is three people old.

scenarios.debrief: The whole case turned on a repeat tracing that nobody ordered. Serial 12-leads every 15 to 30 minutes during ongoing chest pain exist because roughly a third of infarcts are invisible on the first recording, and the change is often the earliest evidence there is. Two specifics ride along with it. Inferior elevation means a right-sided tracing before nitroglycerin, because a right ventricle that cannot generate its own pressure depends on filling and a vasodilator can collapse it; V4R sits at the 5th intercostal space in the right midclavicular line and 0.5 mm there is diagnostic. And every tracing travels: the normal one establishes the timeline, the abnormal one establishes the diagnosis, and the labeled extra-lead study establishes why the drug was withheld. Time, initials, and a plain-words handoff into an actual hand.
